turn_text: Well, it's always a pleasure to be with you, Kim.
I know you're busy in Washington, but I'm sure your thoughts and prayers are back in Oklahoma with those who were hit by that devastating tornado in Moore.
Absolutely, Kim. The Oklahoma delegation flew yesterday back to Oklahoma, both senators and all five of the House members.

Guard gave us a helicopter tour of the area we were on the ground with Governor Fallon, visiting with folks, visiting with the rescue and recovery people. It's just incredible what Mother Nature can do. It's a miracle with the magnitude of destruction on the 20-mile swath that the casualties weren't 10 or 15 times that much. It's just a miracle. It restores your faith in human nature to know

Oklahomans and I think the same spirit of Greece exists across the country. When our neighbors are hurting, we step up to help them in every way we can and more. We'll put itself back together and they'll bury those who've been lost and they'll move forward. But you just have to have respect from other nature in our part of the world.

Well, let's turn our attention back to Washington DC and the job you do. The House of Representatives went through markup in one day on the AG committee. And I wonder if you'd comment on that process and if you were surprised by anything during the markup session.

Well, I would say probably a lot of people were surprised in that a year ago using an open process regular order letting every member offer their amendments, debate their amendments, secure both a voice voter if they wanted it, a recorded vote. We managed to pass our bill out of committee by a vote of 35, yes, 11, no. That was a majority of both Republicans and Democrats. One year later, we had just about the same number of amendments, a little over 100. We started at the same time at 10 o'clock in the morning. We were out for three and a half hours for conference and floor votes, but yet we still finished three hours quicker, I think, and passed by one vote larger margin. thirty six to ten. I think that says something about the process the committee's gone through in developing consensus and coming to respect each other's opinions and putting a good solid bill together. That's not to say that it didn't have its moments of intense debate. Absolutely there work in. But I think I leave the committee now with an amazingly cohesive group of members both ours and these alike as we move to the floor. Some people will note that Perhaps organic has come of age by the nature of the vote in favor of the amendment dealing with organics. Some were probably surprised that the amendment dealing with the dairy supply language of Mr. Peterson's was not successful in removing the supply management program. But all in all, I think it was a very positive debate on all issues by all members and strengthens our hand as we go to the floor in June.

turn_text: Your committees seem polarized and those who appear to be there to defend and expand the food programs and those who are most concerned with crop insurance and traditional agricultural programs. Is that divide widening?

I don't know that it's widening. I think it's probably becoming more, the various focuses have become more intense. Our listeners need to remember in the last couple of years approximately 80% of all farm bill spending have been the social nutrition programs, school lunch, wick women's infants and children and uh... step affectionately remembered by many of us as food stamps eighty percent of the spending so when you look at the committee itself in all fairness there's a probably about forty percent of the membership who are from inner city districts or districts where the nutritional issues are most important you've got about forty percent of the committee who are like myself from very rural agricultural districts whether it's processing or production side You've got about 20% of the committee who are there for a variety of reasons or because of conservation or because they don't have a clue why they're on the committee. That will happen in any committees, you know, Ken. So the balance is fairly even. So it really shouldn't surprise anybody that when we address the nutrition programs, whether it's Mr. McGovern from Massachusetts, a Democrat on the committee or a number of others, there's a lot of very intense emotion there. And from myself as a cow-calf wheat guy in Western Oklahoma,

am very, very focused on making sure that the 20% of the bill that some would say actually raises the food and fiber we need in this country and around the world. I'm very, very intense on that. So we'll ultimately come to a consensus. We did buy 36 of the 46 members voting yes on the final draft the other night.
Could you give me a bit of logistics of what you think will take place when the bill will come to the floor and any indication of the rules for debate and the number of amendments?

Ken, leadership tells me that we'll come to the floor in June out. They've not given me a specific date. But if you look at the calendar, when we're in session, when we're not in session, if you look at the kind of the flow of things, I would predict, and it's a strictly speculation on my part, I would predict probably the middle part of June. So essentially a month from now as we speak. The house by the nature of the way we do legislation, every bill that comes to the floor has to have a special rule. And that rule defines how much debate time, that rule defines will amendments be in order, how many amendments will be in order, what's the process by which the amendments will be offered, the time allotments for each amendment, all of those sort of things. I have begun the process of visiting with the leadership to try to convince them that in a bill, the nature of the farm bill and a bill where a vast majority of the members of the House of Representatives as a whole have a very limited understanding of the farm bill. We need a rule that says that two or three days before the bill is considered on the floor that amendments need to be filed, a filing requirement. So we all together can have time to figure out what my colleagues are up to. I have advocated and I'm continuing to advocate to my leadership that when the Rules Committee meets that I understand there's a diversity of opinions that we need to have amendments on all the major areas of interest to the body as a whole. I accept that. But can instead of 100 amendments on the floor of the United States House or 120 or 140 are unlimited, what I'm advocating to leadership is Pick out 20 amendments or 30 amendments or 40 amendments. Evenly spread out over the areas of the bill, very definitive, straightforward, understandable amendments. Make those in order so that we can have a real understandable debate that the issues really will make a difference. For instance, potentially, I think there could be an amendment made in order by some of my more conservative colleagues to block grant the entire food stamp program back to the states. And that's been discussed by a number of my colleagues, and there have been letters circulated, but that would be a very straightforward. Do you want to take the federal government out of the Food Stamp Program business and give it to the 50 states? Here's your vote. By the same token from my more liberal colleagues in the United States House, I suspect they would have an amendment to take the $20 billion in reforms we have in nutrition and abolish those. Just keep spending that same amount of money. In all fairness, they probably deserve a vote on that amendment. Things like that. I think probably floor deserves a vote on the supply management portion of the dairy title, which Mr. Peterson crafted over, I guess, a four-year period. The members deserve a vote on that, which was, as you remember, a very contentious topic in committee itself. I guess what I'm just simply saying is don't give me 20 amendments in a row on my new changes in food stamps. Let's have a reasonable number of amendments that make real policy changes that members can really understand and we can really debate the consequences. And then I think the membership will make good decisions.

I would tell you that the bean counters, the fiscal hawks, whatever you want to call them will go after crop insurance because that's really the only major amount of money left. We will, those of us on the committee, and I think Ken, those of us in the body as a whole who understand the importance of crop insurance to production agriculture, the fact that it is in effect now the safety net will fight that. Just as I noticed, The Senate will be battling on the floor of these kind of amendments. So we will struggle with those on the 49 states house. I personally think that we hold the line because it is explainable. I think it will be understandable to the membership why federal crop insurance exists. Because after all, there are a lot of flood insurance programs around the country. There's lots of insurance programs that deal with hurricanes. There's lots of things out there that the federal government does in all other sectors of the American economy. to try and prevent catastrophe. And that's what crop insurance is all about in the farm bill, prevent agricultural catastrophe.
